hints: Look at the South Africa column in Table 2.1 and pick out which of the three Northern European breeds has the highest mean daily milk yield there to replace the native goat.
Remember that how many times greater means the extra yield divided by the starting yield, so think about how to find increase first then divide by 0.25 kg.
walkthrough:
Pick the right maximum value**
You are replacing a native goat living in South Africa, so you need the breed that performs best in South Africa, not in Europe. In the South Africa column, Saanen is $1.45 \text{ kg}$, British Alpine is $0.75 \text{ kg}$ and Toggenburg is $0.56 \text{ kg}$. So Saanen is the one to use.

Calculate times greater correctly**
Times greater is not just new divided by old. It is increase divided by old. First find the extra milk: $1.45 - 0.25 = 1.20 \text{ kg}$. Then divide by the native yield: $1.20 \div 0.25 = 4.8$. That is already to two significant figures, so the answer is 4.8 times greater.
Final answer: Saanen gives maximum yield in South Africa of $1.45 \text{ kg}$. Increase $= 1.45 - 0.25 = 1.20 \text{ kg}$. Times greater $= 1.20 \div 0.25 = 4.8$ times greater.

hints: Focus on one single column in Table 2.1, so the location and climate are kept the same, and compare what happens to milk yield between the different breeds.
Think about why animals kept in the same environment would still differ - what is different inside them from selective breeding in the past.
walkthrough:
Hold environment constant**
To see genes at work you keep environment the same. Pick any one location, for example South Africa. All three breeds there experience the same climate, vegetation and veterinary care, yet they yield very differently: Saanen $1.45 \text{ kg}$, British Alpine $0.75 \text{ kg}$, Toggenburg $0.56 \text{ kg}$.

Link difference to genes**
If environment is the same, the remaining cause of the difference must be inherited. Different breeds have different gene pools and different alleles for milk production because humans have selectively bred them differently in the past. That is genetic variation showing itself as phenotypic variation.

Final answer: Different breeds kept in the same location have different mean daily milk yields due to different alleles / gene pools from selective breeding. e.g. in South Africa Saanen $1.45 \text{ kg}$ compared to Toggenburg $0.56 \text{ kg}$.

hints: This time keep the genes the same by following one single breed row across the table and see what happens to its yield in the three different locations.
Think about how factors like food supply, temperature stress and disease care could change how much milk the same genes can actually produce.
walkthrough:
Hold genes constant**
Follow one row, for example Saanen. Its genes are the same breed, yet its yield changes a lot: $5.17 \text{ kg}$ in Northern Europe, $1.73 \text{ kg}$ in Barbados and $1.45 \text{ kg}$ in South Africa. Toggenburg shows the same pattern: $4.54 \text{ kg}$ to $0.56 \text{ kg}$.

Link difference to environment**
Because the breed is the same, the change must come from outside the animal. Northern Europe, Barbados and South Africa differ in climate, type and amount of vegetation to eat, and availability of veterinary care. Poorer nutrition, heat stress or more disease can all lower the milk yield that the genes could potentially give.

Final answer: The same breed has different mean daily milk yields in different locations due to different environmental conditions. e.g. Saanen $5.17 \text{ kg}$ in Northern Europe compared to $1.45 \text{ kg}$ in South Africa, due to differences in climate / vegetation for food / veterinary care.

hints: Start by thinking which two parent types you need to cross to bring high milk yield genes and local adaptation genes together in one population.
Consider what the farmer must do after the first cross - which offspring are kept and what happens to the rest.
Think about why one round of breeding is never enough and what must be repeated for many generations.
Remember that milk yield is only seen in females, so think about how you would know if a male carries good milk genes.
Think about a genetic risk of repeatedly breeding close relatives and how to keep the new breed healthy.
walkthrough:
Make the initial cross**
Humans apply artificial selection. Cross a high-yielding Saanen with a local South African goat that is well adapted to heat, local food and diseases. The offspring will carry a mix of alleles for both traits.

Select and breed the best**
From the offspring, choose only those that show both desired characteristics: high milk yield and good survival and health in South Africa. Breed these selected animals together and do not breed the low-yielding or poorly adapted ones.

Repeat over generations**
Repeat this selection and breeding cycle for many generations. Each generation increases the frequency of favourable alleles. This is directional selection toward high yield plus adaptation. Carry out the programme in South Africa so adaptation is tested in the real environment.

Test males and avoid inbreeding**
Males do not produce milk, so use progeny testing: check the milk yield of a male's daughters to decide if he carries good milk alleles. Also avoid mating close relatives and out-cross to unrelated goats to prevent inbreeding depression.

Final answer: Cross Saanen with native South African goat; select offspring with high milk yield and adaptation to local conditions; breed selected offspring together; repeat selection and breeding for many generations; use progeny testing of males by milk yield of daughters; avoid inbreeding by out-crossing.

hints: Think about what lysozyme does to bacteria in unpasteurised milk and how that would directly help the health and growth of children who drink it.
Think about why people might worry about a new human protein in milk, from unknown health effects to cost and willingness to drink it.
walkthrough:
Benefit from killing bacteria**
Lysozyme kills bacteria in the milk, so children drinking unpasteurised milk ingest fewer live pathogens. That means less diarrhoea, better absorption of nutrients and improved growth and development, which is a clear social and health advantage.

Cost from uncertainty and acceptance**
A new human protein in goats milk brings social concerns. Safety risks may be unknown, it could act as an allergen or have side effects, or disturb useful gut bacteria. It may also be expensive to produce, and families may simply refuse to drink GM milk.

Final answer: Advantage: reduces / stops diarrhoea in children or improves nutrition / growth / development. Disadvantage: unknown safety risks / possible allergen / side effects or disrupts gut bacteria or expensive or people unwilling to drink GM milk.
